newsitem.title: UK: LPG falls in all centres as buying interest fades.
newsitem.headline: LPG falls in all centres as buying interest fades.

text.p: European Liquefied Petroleum Gas (LPG) prices fell sharply over the week while levels in Asia drifted off in the absence of significant spot trade, dealers said.
The volume of trade in all centres was limited, reflecting the lack of interest in LPG as a heating fuel in the northern hemisphere summer.
In Europe, trade was limited to small seagoing coasters in the north, with the Mediterranean market thin and little interest heard for full sized cargoes of either propane or butane in any region.
"There's been a total lack of trade on big propane or butane, and no firm talk," a Scandinavian trader said.
Small butane coasters lost around $10 a tonne in the first three days of the week, and were talked in the range $130/$135 a tonne fob NWE by the end of the week.

A trader said that butane prices had fallen to the point at which the product was worth around 90 percent of the naphtha price, so it should start to become competitive with naphtha as an alternative feedstock for petrochemical plants.
"Yesterday and today it's stopped falling any further, and now it should balance," he said.
Propane was also off sharply on the seagoing coaster market. A week ago it was valued near $190 a tonne fob NWE, but is now talked in the low $170's a tonne.
But while small coasters plummeted, the market for large propane cargoes on a delivered basis remained strong, at up to $190 a tonne cif NWE.
"It's still quite firm on big cargoes, very high compared with butane," a trader said. "It must be driven by the storage buying for winter at the end of last month. It's not petchem driven."

At the end of last month a large volume of propane was bought for storage in caverns in Scandinavia, for reselling at higher levels over the winter, dealers said. This has left the market comparatively short and has helped support large propane prices even while the same material in smaller cargoes has slipped.

Lack of buying interest from Japan has reduced the premium over the Saudi Contract Price (CP), the benchmark price against which most Asian LPG is traded, a Japanese trader said. And the discount to the CP on the fob Middle East Gulf market is also falling, he said.

Japanese buyers are bidding around CP +$15 a tonne C+F Japan for propane, he said, with sellers slightly higher than this. And a price of around CP -$10 a tonne fob Middle East Gulf is being discussed for propane, with little interest seen.

"People are waiting for Aramco acceptances before they will start to trade again," said a trader. Saudi Aramco announces acceptances, or the percentages of contractual cargoes that it will be able to deliver, every month, and spot trade is often slow before dealers are informed of these.

A major industry conference in Singapore has kept many players out of the market for most of the week, a dealer said, making it difficult to find serious discussion of market activity. But butane prices have been slightly firmer than propane levels, as a large tender from India has supported the butane price.

In the U.S., spot LPG prices tumbled at the end of the week as bearish stock data and lower crude prices put the market under pressure. Propane stocks in June stood at 47.5 million barrels, up by 17 percent form the same time a year earlier, according to the Energy Information Administration (EIA).

If inventories continue to build at normal rates for the rest of the stock building season, stocks will reach 60 million barrels by the start of the 1997/1998 heating season, the highest level at that time of year since 1994, the EIA said.
